answer: The passage itself was not provided, so this answer draws on the node2vec paper (Grover & Leskovec, 2016). node2vec runs in two main phases: (1) generating biased second-order random walks, and (2) learning embeddings by optimizing a skip-gram objective with stochastic gradient descent, as in word2vec. Its cost is roughly linear in the number of walks, the walk length, and the embedding dimensionality. Preprocessing the transition probabilities (alias tables for each edge) adds overhead that grows with the sum of squared node degrees, and it is a memory cost. The paper describes the walk-simulation phase as parallelizable, since walks from different start nodes are independent and can run concurrently. The optimization phase is parallelized with asynchronous SGD (Hogwild-style updates, as in word2vec), which lets many threads update the embedding matrix with little locking. Thus both major phases can be parallelized, and the authors report that this keeps the method scalable to large networks.
